extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating whether a patent application specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a): i.e., whether the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention as of the filing date. Covers core standard, evidentiary means of showing possession, special-case rules (genus, species, biological materials, means-plus-function), and examiner procedure for making rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Standard — specification must convey possession
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fundamental test asks whether 'the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, the inventor was in possession of the invention as now claimed.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant demonstrates possession by describing the claimed invention with all its limitations using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention. Evaluation is from the perspective of a person skilled in the art as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description separate from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement is 'separate and distinct from the enablement requirement' and serves to demonstrate the inventor actually possessed the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate enablement (whether one can make and use the invention) with written description (whether the inventor was in possession of the claimed subject matter). Both requirements may be analyzed independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequacy and examiner burden
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that adequate written description exists when the application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner bears the initial burden of presenting evidence explaining why a skilled artisan would not recognize that the description supports the claims. Examiners must establish a prima facie case rather than rely on conclusory statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-literal support allowed (not in haec verba)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not use identical language (in haec verba) to be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description is adequate if a skilled artisan would understand the inventor possessed the invention even if the exact claim phrasing is not present. Examiners should evaluate whether support is express, implicit, or inherent, not require verbatim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession may be shown through concrete evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by actual reduction to practice; drawings or chemical formulas; or identifying characteristics such as structure, physical/chemical properties, or functional characteristics with established structure-function correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: constructing an embodiment that meets all claim limitations (reduction to practice); detailed structural depictions in drawings or formulas; identifying characteristics that, given an established structure-function correlation, make clear the inventor had the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single species/embodiment claims require complete support
rubrics_metrics.description: Single species or single embodiment claims must show complete structure, reduction to drawings, or sufficient identifying characteristics distinguishing the species/embodiment from other materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims to a single species, the specification should provide enough detail (structure, drawings, or identifying characteristics) so that a skilled artisan recognizes the claimed species as the inventor's possession and can distinguish it from others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims require representative species or equivalent proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus claims require disclosure of a 'representative number of species' reflecting the genus variation, unless one species alone demonstrates the inventor possessed the broader genus (a fact-dependent inquiry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad genus claims cannot ordinarily be supported by disclosure of only a single species in unpredictable arts unless substantial evidence shows the inventor possessed the entire genus. Examiner should consider predictability of the art and the number/nature of disclosed species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological materials and deposit limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological materials may rely on deposits under 37 CFR 1.801 et seq., but deposits do not substitute for written description—the written disclosure must be as complete as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a deposit can provide access to a biological material, the specification itself must still meet written description requirements. Cross-reference the deposit rules but do not treat a deposit as automatically satisfying written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims require corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claims must disclose adequate corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the claimed function; indefinite means-plus-function claims also lack written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A purely functional recitation without disclosure of structure (or materials/acts) corresponding to that function will typically fail the written description requirement. Examiner should identify missing corresponding structure when evaluating such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement for new or amended claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For new or amended claims, each limitation must be 'expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are amended or added, examiners must verify that every claim limitation finds support in the original filing. Lack of such support can justify a written description rejection or a refusal to accord priority to an earlier filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority/benefit claim support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter must be disclosed in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) in the earlier-filed application to receive that earlier filing date for priority/benefit purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an applicant asserts priority to an earlier application, the earlier disclosure must meet written description standards for the specific subject matter asserted. Examiner should assess whether the earlier application itself provided adequate written description of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical limitations and common written description failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims omitting elements described as essential to the invention lack adequate description; broad genus claims may be unsupported by a single species in unpredictable arts; functional description alone typically fails absent established structure-function correlation; generic disclosure of a broad class does not necessarily support specific compounds or species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for omitted 'critical' elements that the specification treats as essential. Be wary where only functional language is provided without structural correlation, or where a generic disclosure attempts to cover specific chemical/biological species without adequate species-level support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner methodology for making a written description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a written description rejection, the examiner must: (1) identify specific claim limitations lacking support; (2) establish a prima facie case explaining why skilled artisans would not recognize possession; (3) base findings on substantive law, not procedural guidelines; (4) respond thoroughly to applicant arguments and evidence upon reply; and (5) consider the nature of the invention and state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide reasoned, evidence-based findings rather than conclusory assertions (a general assertion of 'unpredictability in the art' alone is insufficient). After applicant reply, examiners should address arguments and any evidence submitted and reassess the prima facie case in view of the record.
